title: 143 Influence of Comfort on performance and carcass characteristics in Akaushi steers and heifers in the feedyard
content:
Abstract
Comfort (COMF; Ralco Agriculture; Marshall, MN) is a feed additive for ruminants formulated with a blend of essential oils and capsicum. The objective of this study was to evaluate the influence of COMF on growth, feedyard performance, and carcass characteristics in Akaushi and Akaushi crossbred steers and heifers during the feedlot phase. Fifty-six Akaushi and Akaushi crossbred steers and heifers were transported 8 h to West Texas A&M’s Research Feedyard (Canyon, TX). Upon arrival calves were weighed, ultrasound scanned and divided into equal treatments. Control pens received no Comfort supplement (CON), while treatment pens received 0.23 kg/hd/d Comfort supplement (COMF) top-dressed. Cattle were fed a receiving ration for 67 days then transitioned to a finishing diet for duration of the trial. Cattle were scanned via ultrasound for ribeye area (REAU), fat thickness (FTU), rump fat (RFU), and intramuscular fat (IMFU) on d 0, 59, 115, 168, and 227. In addition, ultrasound of jugular vein occurred on d 115, 168 and 227. Statistical analysis was conducted using PROC MIXED procedure in SAS, with d treated as a repeated measure. Model included treatment and sex as fixed effects. Experimental unit was defined as pen (n = 12). There was no difference in starting weight between treatment groups (P = 0.95), but a significant difference between sexes (P = 0.02). Gain to feed from d 0-59 for COMF tended to be higher than CON (0.12 vs 0.09; P = 0.06) but was not different between d 60-301 (P = 0.42). Body weight on d 59 was numerically higher for COMF cattle (346.5 vs. 327.0 kg; P = 0.11), although final BW was not different between treatments (607.4 COMF vs. 605.1 kg CON; P = 0.89). During the receiving period, ADG tended to increase for COMF treatment (1.23 vs 0.97 kg; P = 0.08), and ADG was significantly higher for CON in finishing period (1.08 vs 1.15 kg; P = 0.02). There was a tendency for increased DMI in CON cattle compared to cattle fed COMF from d 60 to 301 (8.83 vs 8.41 kg; P = 0.06). There were no differences for FTU, RFU, IMFU, jugular diameter, hot carcass weight, or Longissimus Muscle area between the two treatments. Cattle fed COMF tended to grade USDA Prime more compared to CON (71.7% vs. 44.5%; P = 0.10), thus leading to CON treatment tending to grade USDA Choice more than COMF (55.5% vs. 28.30%; P = 0.10). Additionally, there were not significant differences for USDA Yield grades 2, 3, and 4 (P ≥ 0.17). These results demonstrate that Comfort was most effective in the first 60 d in the feedyard. Comfort positively increased USDA grade and improved cattle performance during times of environmental heat stress.
